title: Meta-Scaling Laws: On the Invariance and Generality of Neural Scaling
claim: Scaling behavior is unchanged under information-preserving transformations but progressively weakens as a transformation discards more information.
layout: 2x3 grid of log-x line plots; top bijective, bottom non-bijective, columns are datasets
description: A two-row, three-column grid of line plots. Columns are the datasets WikiText-103, OpenWebText and C4. Each panel plots test loss (NLL) against dataset size on a log x-axis. The top row, labeled Bijective, shows three marker series (Standard as red stars, Linear as blue diamonds, Non-linear as green squares) that nearly overlap. Black dash-dotted power-law fits run through them, and faint thin lines show individual model sizes. The bottom row, labeled Non-Bijective, shows Standard plus quantization levels ρ(T)=0.75, 0.50 and 0.25 (blue diamonds, green squares, purple triangles). These curves are clearly separated vertically, and the lower the ρ, the lower and flatter the curve. The overlap in the top row against the stacked, flattening curves in the bottom row is what the eye notices first. Subpanel captions (a) to (f) sit under each plot.
caption: NSLs for language modeling on the WikiText (left), OpenWebText (middle), and C4 (right) datasets. The first row presents results under bijective transformations, the second row corresponds to non-bijective transformations (quantization). In the figures, the thin colored lines represent the test loss curves for individual parameter sizes, while the scaling law estimates (black dotted lines) are fitted using the average test loss values across parameter sizes. Results on negative log-likelihood (NLL) indicate that bijective transformations do not alter the scaling behavior; in contrast, as the degree of information loss increases, the scaling behavior progressively weakens.
abstract: Neural scaling laws establish a predictable relationship between model performance and data or compute, offering crucial guidance for resource allocation in new domains and tasks. Yet such laws are most needed precisely where they are hardest to obtain: fitting one for a new model and task pair demands expensive sweeps that typically exhaust the very compute budget the law is meant to economize. We study meta-scaling laws: relations that characterize when neural scaling behavior is preserved and predict how it changes under data transformations, enabling forecasts across domains when the shift can be approximated by a compatible transformation. We address this by identifying the right invariants: scaling laws are preserved under bijective (information-preserving) transformations of the data and modified in predictable, information-theoretically grounded ways under non-bijective transformations that lower its information resolution $Ï$: a single axis along which a law fit in one domain can be transported to another. We validate this across language, vision, and speech, and demonstrate two cross-domain applications: predicting scaling for language models trained on electronic health records from laws fit on general text, and predicting time-series classification scaling under varying levels of noise injection, recovering the data-scaling exponents to within $3\%$ error.
